title_en: In Praise of the Discovery of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross
author: Alexander Monachus
addressee: Orthodox Christian faithful celebrating the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross
occasion: A festal oration for the anniversary of the finding and exaltation of the Cross, retelling how Constantine and Helena recovered the holy places and ending in praise of the Cross.
argument: The work opens by setting the scene under Bishop Macarius of Aelia and Emperor Constantine, whose laws establish Christian peace until Arius disturbs the churches. Constantine summons the Council of Nicaea, then sends his mother Helena to Jerusalem to search for the Cross and holy places. Helena orders the demolition of the pagan shrine, the tomb and three crosses are found, and Bishop Macarius identifies the true Cross by bringing each cross to a dying woman, who is healed by the true one. Part of the Cross and the nails are sent to Constantine, churches are commissioned, and the feast of the Cross is established. The oration closes with a long rhetorical praise of the Cross and a doxological prayer.

outline.move: Introduces Macarius of Aelia and Constantine's Christian laws, then recounts the Arian disturbance and the Council of Nicaea, after which Constantine commissions Macarius to seek the Cross and sends Helena to Jerusalem.

Narrates the search for the Cross, Helena's order to demolish the pagan shrine, the discovery of the tomb and three crosses, Macarius's healing miracle that identifies the true Cross, and the sending of relics to Constantine, followed by the building of churches and the establishment of the feast.

Defends the accuracy of the preceding account by asserting that no other bishop of Jerusalem, no other Roman emperor, and no other manner of finding the Cross existed; fixes the feast date; and begins a long series of acclamations praising the Cross.
Continues the praise of the Cross, cites prophets, apostles, and martyrs, and concludes with an exhortation to celebrate the feast and a doxological prayer.

cast.name: Macarius
cast.who: Bishop of Aelia (Jerusalem), successor of Hermonas, who oversees the finding of the Cross and performs the healing miracle that identifies it.

cast.name: Constantine
cast.who: Roman emperor who becomes sole ruler, convenes Nicaea, and commissions the search for the Cross.

cast.name: Helena
cast.who: Constantine's mother, who travels to Jerusalem and directs the discovery of the Cross and building of churches.

cast.name: Arius
cast.who: Alexandrian whose teaching disturbs the churches and is condemned at Nicaea.

cast.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
cast.who: Bishop who follows Arius and is exiled after Nicaea.

cast.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
cast.who: Bishop associated with Arius's party, traditionally called Eusebius Pamphili (Eusebius, son of Pamphilus), the church historian.

cast.name: Hermonas
cast.who: Previous bishop of Aelia, succeeded by Macarius; the source gives the name in the accusative case.

cast.name: Maximonas
cast.who: Macarius's successor as bishop of Aelia, a confessor who lost his right eye in persecution.

scripture: The author cites the Old Testament in Greek, following Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering. Quotations should be identified by modern English Bible references using standard Protestant or ecumenical names, with Septuagint Psalm numbering noted where it differs from the Hebrew.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Eusebius of Caesarea, source_forms: ["Εὐσέβιος ὁ Παμφίλου"], who: "Bishop associated with Arius's party, traditionally called Eusebius Pamphili (Eusebius, son of Pamphilus), the church historian."
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source reads Εὐσέβιος ὁ Παμφίλου, which means "Eusebius [the one] of Pamphilus" (i.e., Eusebius Pamphili). The brief correctly identifies this as Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, but the parenthetical "(Eusebius, son of Pamphilus)" is slightly misleading: ὁ Παμφίλου is a genitive of relationship (son of Pamphilus), not a patronymic adjective. More importantly, the brief's description "the church historian" is an identification not supported by the source text, which gives no indication of which Eusebius this is beyond his association with Arius's party.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Helena (reported motivation), how_marked: "Participial clause introduced by αὐτῆς... αἰτησάσης and φασκούσης describing her request and claim, not direct or indirect quoted speech"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: αὐτῆς τοῦτο αἰτησάσης τῆς βασιλίδος, φασκούσης ὀπτασίαν τινὰ θείαν ἑωρακέναι κελεύουσαν αὐτῇ τὰ Ἱεροσόλυμα καταλαβεῖν, καὶ τοὺς ἁγίους τόπους εἰς φῶς ἀγαγεῖν χωσθέντας ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνέμων, καὶ ἀφανεῖς γεγονότας ἐπὶ τοσούτους χρόνους
_unresolved_facts.fix: The participial clause is introduced by αὐτῆς... αἰτησάσης τῆς βασιλίδος, φασκούσης, but the content of what Helena claims is presented in indirect statement with the infinitive ἑωρακέναι and its accusative subject ὀπτασίαν, with a further participial clause κελεύουσαν... So it is indirect reported speech (indirect statement with infinitive), not merely "describing her request and claim" without quotation. The brief should say: "Indirect reported speech in an accusative-and-infinitive construction dependent on φασκούσης, with participial clause."

_unresolved_facts.claim: Scripture (quoted), how_marked: "Introduced by quotation formulas such as λέγοντος and φησιν"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: λέγοντος· «Ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ, ἔσται τὸ ἐπὶ τὸν χαλινὸν τοῦ ἵππου, ἅγιον Κυρίῳ παντοκράτορι.»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief says "λέγοντος and φησιν" but φησιν in the source (ὥς φασιν οἱ περὶ ταῦτα δεινοὶ) introduces a technical explanation about πυκάζοντα, not a scriptural quotation. The scriptural quotations are introduced by: (1) λέγοντος (referring to the Lord speaking through the prophet), (2) no explicit formula for the Psalm quotation in the acclamations (Ἔδωκας τοῖς φοβουμένοις σε...), (3) δι' ἑνὸς αὐτῶν ἱεροκήρυκος for Galatians 6:14, and (4) φησιν ἡ θεία Γραφή for the exhortation to celebrate. The brief should not list φησιν alone as a quotation formula for scripture without qualification, and should note that some quotations lack introductory formulas.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Bishop Macarius identifies the true Cross by bringing each cross to a dying woman, who is healed by the true one
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὁ δὲ ἐπίσκοπος διὰ πίστεως τὴν διάκρισιν ἔλυσεν. Γυναικὶ γὰρ ἀῤῥωστούσῃ τῶν ἐμφανῶν, καὶ ἀπεγνωσμένῃ ὑπὸ πάντων, καὶ τὰ τελευταῖα πνεούσῃ, προσαγαγὼν ἑκάτερον τῶν σταυρῶν, τὸν ζητούμενον ηὗρεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says προσαγαγὼν ἑκάτερον τῶν σταυρῶν ("bringing each of the two crosses"), not "each cross" implying all three. The source mentions three crosses were found (τρεῖς σταυροὶ κεχωρισμένοι), but the bishop tests only two (ἑκάτερον). The brief should say "bringing each of the two crosses" or "bringing two crosses" rather than "each cross."

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-mid move: "Defends the accuracy of the preceding account by asserting that no other bishop of Jerusalem, no other Roman emperor, and no other manner of finding the Cross existed"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐπίσκοπος ἕτερος Ἱεροσολύμων γέγονε πώποτε παρὰ τοὺς προγεγραμμένους, οὐδὲ βασιλεὺς ἕτερος Ῥωμαίων, οὐδὲ μὴν ἑτέρῳ τρόπῳ ὁ τίμιος σταυρὸς εὑρέθη.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says "no other bishop of Jerusalem ever existed besides those previously written" (not "no other manner of finding the Cross existed" in the sense of method). The brief's "no other manner of finding the Cross existed" overinterprets ἑτέρῳ τρόπῳ. The claim is that the Cross was not found in another way (i.e., by other people or at another time), not about the manner/method of finding. Better: "no other bishop of Jerusalem, no other Roman emperor, and the Cross was not found in any other way."

The source uses "Αἰλίας" and "Αἰλίᾳ" for the episcopal see (ὁ τῆς Αἰλίας ἐπίσκοπος), which is Aelia Capitolina, the Roman name for Jerusalem. However, the source also uses "Ἱεροσόλυμα" (Jerusalem) multiple times for the city itself. The brief's equation of Aelia with Jerusalem is conventional but oversimplified: in this text, "Aelia" refers specifically to the episcopal see/title (Bishop of Aelia), while "Jerusalem" is used for the city. The brief should note this distinction or use "Aelia (the see corresponding to Jerusalem)".
